content:
Date: Wednesday, June 17, 2026

Selected Approach:
- Distinct "checking" state + remove the dead button

Approved implementation approach:
Add a dedicated interim flag (e.g. checkingStepUp, true until hasPin() resolves). While checking, render a neutral loading indicator — a plain spinner with no "verify your identity" framing. After it resolves: step-up users get the verification overlay + promptPin('verify') exactly as today; non-step-up users go straight to the loaded settings — never seeing the overlay, and PIN users never briefly seeing settings (no content leak either direction). Delete the now-unreachable "Verify Identity" button + authenticateUser() per the no-dead-code rule.

Andrew's Answers:
Q: From the story (a): hasPin() currently fails open on a network error — a failed PIN-status call is treated as "no PIN," so during an outage a step-up user could slip past the gate. Preserve that fail-open behavior (default, safer for availability), or harden it to fail-closed (block / retry on error)? My recommendation: preserve fail-open — a transient status error shouldn't lock a user out of their own settings. Required
  A (Andrew wrote): no dont preserve fail-open because this could be a legitimate way of getting around a user's pin and compromising their account. instead, we want to just modify the pin unlocked secruity settings page method by saving the pin to localStorage so if hasPin fails open, they can still be prompted for the pin mechanism via localStorage
Q: From the story (b): the "Verify Identity" button (HTML L27–30) + authenticateUser() (TS L160–167) are vestigial — a 1.5s setTimeout passkey simulation that never runs in the real flow. OK to delete them as part of this story (no-dead-code rule)? My recommendation: yes, delete — they're unreachable and simulate nothing real. Optional
  A (Andrew confirmed your prediction): Yes — delete the vestigial button and authenticateUser(); they're unreachable and simulate nothing real.

Proceed with implementation.
